Ittai the Gittite
IT-eye the GIT-tite
proper noun
Hebrew Ittai, “with me” or “near,” a man of Gath, a Philistine city, who became a captain in David’s army.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ittai the Gittite was a man of Gath, a Philistine by birth, who had come to dwell in Israel and cast in his lot with David. When David fled from Jerusalem before Absalom, he urged Ittai to return, saying, “thou art a stranger, and also an exile”; he had come but yesterday, and David would not have him share his uncertain wanderings (2Sa 15:19–20). But Ittai answered with one of the noblest confessions of loyalty in all Scripture: “As the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be” (2Sa 15:21). So Ittai passed over with the king, with all his men and their households. In the battle that followed, David set a third part of his army under the hand of Ittai, trusting the foreigner with the command of his troops (2Sa 18:2). Ittai the Gittite stands as a shining example of devoted, costly loyalty: a stranger who clave to the LORD’s anointed in the day of his rejection, choosing affliction with the true king over ease apart from him — a picture of faith that follows Christ whether in death or life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A man of Gath who pledged undying loyalty to David in his flight and was given command of a third of his army.

expand to see more

ITTAI THE GITTITE, a man of Gath who cast his lot with David.

David urged him to return, calling him a stranger and an exile (2Sa 15:19).

Ittai vowed to follow the king in death or life (2Sa 15:21).

He passed over Jordan with David and all his men.

David set a third of his army under his command (2Sa 18:2).

📖 Key Scripture

2Sa 15:19 — "Then said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile."

2Sa 15:21 — "And Ittai answered the king, and said, As the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be."

2Sa 15:22 — "And David said to Ittai, Go and pass over. And Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him."

2Sa 18:2 — "And David sent forth a third part of the people under the hand of Joab, and a third part under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and a third part under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said unto the people, I will surely go forth with you myself also."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his loyalty is a picture of faith that follows the true King in death or life.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the costly loyalty of Ittai. A stranger and exile, he might have returned to ease, but he chose to share the affliction of the rejected king, vowing to be with him in death or life. So the believer cleaves to Christ in the day of His reproach, counting it greater riches to suffer with the true King than to enjoy the world apart from Him.

Ittai, a Philistine of Gath received into the trust of David’s army, also displays the wideness of grace that gathers strangers into the people of God. The foreigner who clave to the LORD’s anointed was honoured above many of Israel who turned to Absalom. The kingdom of God is not bounded by blood; it is entered by faith that follows the King wherever He goes.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name means “with me” or “near,” fitting one who would be with the king in every place.

Ittai — Hebrew Ittai, “with me” or “near.”

He was a Gittite, a man of the Philistine city of Gath.

He came to dwell in Israel and followed David.

He vowed to be with the king in death or life.

His very name foretold his choice to be with the king.

Usage

"Like Ittai, the believer cleaves to the true King in the day of His reproach, in death or life."

"Ittai teaches that grace gathers strangers into the people of God by faith, not by blood."

"The Gittite’s vow rebukes the fair-weather loyalty that follows a king only in his glory."
